questions.stem:
The table below shows the distances (to the nearest km) travelled to work by the 50 employees in an office.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Distance (km)} & \text{Frequency (f)} & \text{Distance midpoint }(x)\\ \hline 0-2 & 16 & 1.25\\ \hline 3-5 & 12 & 4\\ \hline 6-10 & 10 & 8\\ \hline 11-20 & 8 & 15.5\\ \hline 21-40 & 4 & 30.5\\ \hline\end{array}$

[You may use $\sum fx = 394$, $\sum fx^2 = 6500$]

A histogram has been drawn to represent these data.

The bar representing the distance of $3-5$ has a width of 1.5 cm and a height of 6 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the width and height of the bar representing the distance of $6-10$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Width $= \frac{5}{3}\times 1.5 = \underline{2.5}$ (cm) B1
Area $= 6\times 1.5 = 9\text{ cm}^2$ has frequency $=12$ so $1.5\text{ cm}^2 = 2$ people (o.e.) M1
Frequency of 10 corresponds to area of 7.5 so height $= \underline{3}$ (cm) A1
Notes: M1 for forming a relationship between area and no. of people or "their width" $\times$ "their height" = 7.5, or for $\frac{3h}{10}=\frac{9}{12}$ oe. A1 for height of 3 (cm). NOTE: the common incorrect answer width = 3 and height = 2.5 scores B0M1A0

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median distance travelled to work.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $Q_2 = [2.5+]\frac{(25/25.5-16)}{12}\times 3 = 4.75$ (or 4.875 if use $n+1$) awrt $\underline{4.75}$ M1 A1
Notes: M1 for a correct fraction $[\frac{9}{12}$ or $\frac{9.5}{12}]\times 3$. Ignore end point but must be +. May be seen in an equivalent expression e.g. $\frac{(x-2.5)}{5.5-2.5}=\frac{25-16}{28-16}$. Allow use of $(n+1)$ giving 4.875. NB May work down so look out for $[5.5]-\frac{28-25}{12}\times 3$, etc.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) (i) Show that an estimate of the mean distance travelled to work is 7.88 km.
(ii) Estimate the standard deviation of the distances travelled to work.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) $[\bar{x}=]\frac{394}{50}=7.88$ (*) B1cso
(ii) $[\sigma_x=]\sqrt{\frac{6500}{50}-\bar{x}^2}=\sqrt{67.9056}$ M1A1
$=$ awrt $\underline{8.24}$ (Accept $s=$ awrt 8.32) A1
Notes: (i) B1 for $\frac{394}{50}$ or for fully correct expression seen $\frac{16\times 1.25+12\times 4+10\times 8+8\times 15.5+4\times 30.5}{50}$. (ii) M1 for a correct expression must have 6500, 50 and 7.88 (square root not necessary for M1). 1st A1 for a correct expression which must have square root. 2nd A1 for awrt 8.24 (use of $s=$ awrt 8.32). Condone incorrect labelling if awrt 8.24 is found.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Describe, giving a reason, the skewness of these data.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\bar{x} > Q_2$ B1ft
So positive (skew) dB1
Notes: 1st B1ft for a correct comparison of $\bar{x}=7.88$ and their $Q_2$ (this may be seen embedded in another formula i.e. 3(mean-median)/s.d.). $Q_3-Q_2>Q_2-Q_1$ is B0 unless $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ have been found. ($Q_1=1.95/1.99$, $Q_3=10.25/10.81$). 2nd dB1 dependent on the 1st B1 and for concluding "positive" skew. Note: if their $Q_2>7.88$, then B0. Positive correlation is B0.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Peng starts to work in this office as the 51st employee.

She travels a distance of 7.88 km to work.

(e) Without carrying out any further calculations, state, giving a reason, what effect Peng's addition to the workforce would have on your estimates of the

(i) mean,

(ii) median,

(iii) standard deviation

of the distances travelled to work.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e)(i) There is no effect on the mean B1
(ii) The median will increase B1
(iii) The standard deviation will decrease B1

questions.stem:
The random variable $Y \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$

Given that $\mathrm{P}(Y<17)=0.6$ find

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{P}(Y>17)=1-\mathrm{P}(Y<17)=\underline{0.4}$ B1
Note: do not isw if 0.6554 is given as answer after 0.4 has been seen.

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu)=0.5$ or $[\mathrm{P}(\mu<Y<17)=]0.6-0.5$ M1
$=\underline{0.1}$ A1
Note: M1 for indicating $\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu)=0.5$ (may be seen on a diagram)

parts.label: c
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu \mid Y<17)=]\frac{\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu)}{\mathrm{P}(Y<17)}$ or $\frac{0.5}{0.6}$ M1
$=\frac{5}{6}$ awrt $\underline{0.833}$ A1
Note: M1 for a correct statement $\frac{\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu)}{\mathrm{P}(Y<17)}$ or a correct ratio of probabilities. May be implied by $\frac{\mathrm{P}(Y<\mu)}{0.6}$ or $\frac{0.5}{\mathrm{P}(Y<17)}$

questions.stem:
The Venn diagram below shows the probabilities of customers having various combinations of a starter, main course or dessert at Polly's restaurant.

$S$ = the event a customer has a starter.

$M$ = the event a customer has a main course.

$D$ = the event a customer has a dessert.

The Venn diagram shows: $S$ only $= p$, $S\cap M$ only $=0.17$, $M$ only $=q$, $S\cap M\cap D=0.10$, $S\cap D$ only $=0.04$, $M\cap D$ only $=0.15$, $D$ only $=0.06$, outside all circles $=0$.

Given that the events $S$ and $D$ are statistically independent

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{P}(S)=0.31+p$, $\mathrm{P}(D)=0.35$, $\mathrm{P}(S\cap D)=0.14$ M1
$(0.31+p)(0.35)=0.14$ oe M1
$\mathrm{P}(S)=0.4$ or $0.31+p=0.4$ or $0.35p=0.0315$ A1
$p=\underline{0.09}$ A1
Notes: 1st M1 for attempting $\mathrm{P}(S)$, $\mathrm{P}(D)$ and $\mathrm{P}(S\cap D)$ with at least 2 correct. These may be seen in a conditional probability. NB $\mathrm{P}(S\mid D)=\frac{0.14}{0.35}$ and $\mathrm{P}(D\mid S)=\frac{0.14}{0.31+p}$. 2nd M1 using the independence condition and their values to form a suitable equation for $p$ or $\mathrm{P}(S)$. 1st A1 for $\mathrm{P}(S)=0.4$ or $0.31+p=0.4$ or $0.35p=0.0315$ (i.e. one move from $p=\ldots$)

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{P}(S\cup M\cup D)=1$ so $q=1-(0.17+0.10+0.15+0.06+0.04)-p$ or $0.48-p$ M1
$q=\underline{0.39}$ A1ft
Notes: M1 for using sum of probabilities = 1 and ft their $p$. A1ft for $0.48-$"their $p$" (provided $0<$their $p<0.48$)

parts.label: c
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) $[\mathrm{P}(D\mid S\cap M)=]\frac{\mathrm{P}(D\cap S\cap M)}{\mathrm{P}(S\cap M)}=\frac{0.10}{0.27}$ M1
$=\frac{10}{27}$ or awrt $\underline{0.370}$ A1
(ii) $[\mathrm{P}(D\mid S'\cap M)=]\frac{\mathrm{P}(D\cap S'\cap M)}{\mathrm{P}(S'\cap M)}=\frac{0.15}{0.54}$ M1
$=\frac{5}{18}$ or awrt $\underline{0.278}$ A1
Notes: 1st M1 for a correct ratio of probabilities or a correct ratio expression with at least one correct probability substituted. (M0 if numerator is $\mathrm{P}(D)\times \mathrm{P}(S\cap M)$ or numerator>denominator). 2nd M1 for a correct ratio of probabilities or a correct ratio expression with at least one correct probability substituted. (M0 if numerator is $\mathrm{P}(D)\times \mathrm{P}(S'\cap M)$ or numerator>denominator)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st A1 for $\frac{10}{27}$ or awrt 0.370
- 2nd A1 for $\frac{5}{18}$ or awrt 0.278

parts.label: d
parts.text:
One evening 63 customers are booked into Polly's restaurant for an office party. Polly has asked for their starter and main course orders before they arrive.

Of these 63 customers

27 ordered a main course and a starter,

36 ordered a main course without a starter.

(d) Estimate the number of desserts that these 63 customers will have.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) 27 order $S\cap M$ so expect $27\times \frac{10}{27}$ $D$ or 36 order $S'\cap M$ so expect $36\times \frac{5}{18}$ $D$ M1
So expect $\underline{20}$ (desserts) A1cao
Note: M1 for at least one correct calculation ft their probabilities from (c) i.e. either $27\times$their (c)(i) or $36\times$their (c)(ii)

questions.stem: One event at Pentor sports day is throwing a tennis ball. The distance a child throws a tennis ball is modelled by a normal distribution with mean 32 m and standard deviation 12 m. Any child who throws the tennis ball more than 50 m is awarded a gold certificate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that, to 3 significant figures, 6.68% of children are awarded a gold certificate.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $[\mathrm{P}(D>50)=]\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{50-32}{12}\right)$ M1
$=1-\mathrm{P}(Z<1.5)$ or $1-0.9332$ M1
$=$ awrt $\underline{0.0668}$ or 6.68% A1cso
Notes: 1st M1 for standardising with 50, 32 and 12. Allow $\pm$. 2nd M1 for $1-\mathrm{P}(Z<1.5)$ seen i.e. a correct method for finding $\mathrm{P}(Z>1.5)$ e.g. $1-$ tables value. A1cso for awrt 0.0668 with both Ms scored and no incorrect working seen. Condone incomplete notation and condone use of different letters for $Z$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A silver certificate is awarded to any child who throws the tennis ball more than $d$ metres but less than 50 m.

Given that 19.1% of the children are awarded a silver certificate,

(b) find the value of $d$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{P}(D>d)=0.191+0.0668=0.2578$ or $\mathrm{P}(D<d)=0.7422$ B1
$\frac{d-32}{12}=0.65$ (calc gives $0.65014\ldots$ or $0.65012\ldots$) M1A1
$d=\underline{39.8}$ A1
Notes: B1 for awrt 0.2578 (calc = 0.257807..) or awrt 0.7422 (calc = 0.742192..) may be implied by $z=$ awrt 0.65. M1 for standardising with 32 and 12, i.e. $\pm\frac{d-32}{12}$ (equating to a probability is M0). 1st A1 for $z=$ awrt 0.65 and a correct equation in $d$ (with compatible signs). 2nd A1 for awrt 39.8

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Three children are selected at random from those who take part in the throwing a tennis ball event.

(c) Find the probability that 1 is awarded a gold certificate and 2 are awarded silver certificates. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $0.0668\times 0.191^2\,[=0.0024369\ldots]$ M1
$[\ldots]\times 3$ M1
$=0.00731079\ldots=$ awrt $\underline{0.0073}$ A1
Notes: 1st M1 for $0.0668\times 0.191^2$ or sight of awrt 0.0024 (may be seen embedded in part of an expression, e.g. "$n\times 0.0668\times 0.191^2$") (condone $6.68\%\times 19.1\%\times 19.1\%$ if the final answer given is <1). 2nd M1 for any expression of the form $3pq^2$ where $p$ and $q$ are both probabilities. A1 for awrt 0.0073 allow awrt 0.73% but 0.73 is A0
